title: Two friends at the festival
hookLine: Upatissa and Kolita watch a festival and suddenly find it empty

cards: Same seats as last year. Same hill above the city. Same crowd, same plays, same music, same jokes landing in the same places.

Two young men from good families sit side by side in the best seats, as they always do at this festival. Other years, they laughed at the funny parts, cried at the sad ones and threw gifts to the performers.
This year, the jokes land, and neither of them laughs. The sad scene plays, and neither of them cries. Each glances over and sees the other has gone quiet too.

teach.b: First, the two friends. Their names are Upatissa and Kolita.
The commentaries say they were sons of brahmin families from villages near Rajagaha, close friends since childhood, each with a circle of young companions around him.
Later they'll be known by other names, Sariputta and Moggallana. But not yet. Right now they're two well-off young men at a festival.
Second, the silence. The commentary tells it simply. Kolita turns to his friend: you don't seem to be enjoying yourself today.

teach.h: WHAT IS THERE TO LOOK AT?
teach.b: And Upatissa answers with a question of his own: what is there to look at here? Before long, all these people, the actors, the crowd, the two of them, will be gone. And here we sit, laughing.
Kolita has been thinking the same thing. Neither talked the other into it. They arrived at the same emptiness, in the same seats, on the same afternoon.
Nothing about the festival was worse. What had changed was them. Fourth, the question that's left.

teach.h: A WAY OUT, NOT A WAY HOME.
teach.b: They don't stay sad, and they don't go home and pretend.
They decide, together, to look for a way out of birth and death, a release the festival can't give. Notice how close this sits to the prince's own story.
He saw an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and the palace music went flat. These two never leave their seats. The emptiness finds them in the middle of the fun.

how: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples; in some Theravada temples images of the two stand on either side of the Buddha, and their story is told in sermons and at festivals.

o: the festival held on a hill each year
Sariputta's name, before he became a monk

games.q: the festival on the hill: tap the pairs.

s: only one of the two friends felt the festival was empty
Kolita had been thinking the same thing as Upatissa.
the festival was worse that year
nothing about it had changed; the two friends had.
Upatissa and Kolita are later known as Sariputta and Moggallana
the two friends become the great disciples of the coming days.

games.q: you're at the festival you love, and it suddenly feels empty. your best friend asks what's wrong. what do you do?
o: say you're fine and force a laugh.
tell the truth: what is there to see here?
games.why: Upatissa tells the truth, and finds his friend has been feeling the same thing.

practice: Remember a moment when something meant to be fun went flat, a party, a show, a holiday you'd waited for, and recall the feeling honestly, without judging or fixing it.
Ask what you were hungry for that the fun couldn't give, and let the question rest, unanswered, with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Upatissa. One of two friends who sit through the festival they loved and find it suddenly empty, with his friend Kolita feeling the same. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the show was empty. Two friends, one feeling, and a search about to begin. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

sources.ref: Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada Atthakatha) on verses 11–12, the story of Sariputta and Moggallana
